title: Fundamentals of foundation
summary: Foundation questions are almost always of the form 'which type, and why'. The reliable approach is to identify the problem being solved rather than to memorise a list: weak soil over a large area calls for spreading (raft), a firm stratum out of reach calls for transferring downward (piles), a column at a boundary calls for a strap footing. Learn the pile facts precisely — group spacing, group efficiency, and above all that negative skin friction acts downward as a load, not upward as a resistance.

sections.heading: Requirements and classification
sections.body:
A foundation must satisfy **four** requirements, and a design failing any one is inadequate however well it satisfies the others:

1. **Adequate depth** — below the zone of seasonal moisture change, scour, frost, and any fill or organic layer.
2. **Safety against shear (bearing) failure** — an adequate factor of safety on ultimate bearing capacity, usually **2.5 to 3**.
3. **Settlement within tolerable limits** — both total and, more importantly, **differential**.
4. **Adequate structural strength and durability** — the footing itself must resist the bending and shear induced in it.

Requirements 2 and 3 must both be checked, and **either may govern**. On dense sand, bearing capacity is ample and **settlement governs**; on soft clay, bearing capacity often governs. Assuming one always controls is a standard error.

**Minimum depth** by Rankine's formula:

> **D_min = (q/γ) · [(1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ)]² = (q/γ) · K_a²**

In practice, at least **0.5 m** below ground, and deeper where any of the following applies: seasonal shrink–swell (expansive soil), frost action, scour beside a watercourse, or existing fill.

**Classification:**

| Class | Types | Criterion |
|---|---|---|
| **Shallow** | Isolated, combined, strap, strip, raft | **D_f / B ≤ about 1** |
| **Deep** | Pile, pier, well/caisson | D_f / B > 1, often ≫ 1 |

The distinction is not merely depth: a shallow foundation transfers load **mainly through its base** onto soil near the surface, while a deep foundation transfers it through **shaft friction and end bearing** to strata well below.

**Selecting the type — the discriminator is the problem, not the depth:**

| Problem | Foundation |
|---|---|
| Single column, reasonable soil | **Isolated (spread) footing** |
| Two columns too close for separate footings | **Combined footing** |
| Column at a **boundary**, footing cannot be centred | **Strap (cantilever) footing** |
| A load-bearing **wall** | **Strip / continuous footing** |
| **Weak soil, large loaded area** — footings would cover > ~half the plan | **Raft (mat)** |
| Firm stratum **out of reach** of a shallow foundation | **Piles** |
| Deep water, heavy concentrated load (bridge pier) | **Well / caisson** |
| Very weak soil over a firm stratum, heavy structure | **Pile-supported raft (piled raft)** |

The pairing most often confused is **raft versus piles**. A **raft spreads** load over the greatest available area, and is **shallow**; **piles transfer** load downward to a deeper stratum. Spreading and transferring are different strategies for different problems, and a raft does nothing to reach a deeper stratum.

sections.heading: Shallow foundations
sections.body:
**Isolated footing.** Sized so that the **net pressure** does not exceed the allowable value:

> **A_required = total service load / net allowable bearing pressure**

Then designed structurally for **one-way shear** (checked at **d from the column face**), **two-way punching shear** (on a perimeter **d/2 from the face**, permissible stress **k_s · 0.25√f_ck**), **bending** (critical section at the column face), and **development length** of the reinforcement.

**Punching shear usually governs the thickness** of a footing, not bending — which surprises candidates who size it for moment first.

Footings under the columns of one building should be proportioned for **equal settlement** rather than equal pressure where the loads differ greatly, because it is **differential** settlement that damages a structure.

**Combined and strap footings.** A **combined footing** carries two columns on one base, shaped (rectangular or trapezoidal) so that its **centroid coincides with the resultant of the two column loads** — otherwise the pressure distribution is non-uniform and the footing tilts. A **trapezoidal** shape is used when the loads are unequal and the space is constrained.

A **strap (cantilever) footing** keeps two separate footings but links them with a rigid **strap beam**, which transfers moment from the eccentric boundary footing to the interior one. The strap is designed for **bending only** — it is not intended to bear on the soil, and is often cast clear of it.

**Raft (mat) foundation.** The whole plan area acts as one slab:

> **q = total load / total area**

The rule of thumb: a raft becomes economical when individual footings would cover more than about **half the plan area** — at which point casting one continuous slab is both cheaper and structurally better.

Its **second and often decisive advantage** is that it ties the structure together, greatly reducing **differential** settlement: the raft settles more or less as one body. That matters more than total settlement, because a building settling 50 mm uniformly is undamaged while one settling 10 mm unevenly cracks.

**Types of raft:**

| Type | Form | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Flat plate** | Uniform slab | Light loads, closely spaced columns |
| Plate **thickened under columns** | Local thickening | Where punching shear governs locally |
| **Beam and slab** | Slab stiffened by beams | Heavier or unequal loads |
| **Cellular / box** | Two slabs with intersecting walls | Very stiff, and **buoyant** |
| **Piled raft** | Raft plus piles | Very weak soil, heavy structure |

**The buoyancy (floating) raft** is worth understanding for its ingenuity. Excavating a deep basement **removes a weight of soil**; if that removed weight approaches the weight of the building, the **net increase in pressure at foundation level is near zero**. A heavy building can then be carried on soil that would not otherwise support it. Such a raft must, however, be checked for **uplift**, since an empty basement below the water table can float.

**Design of a raft** proceeds either by the **rigid (conventional) method**, assuming a linear pressure distribution beneath a perfectly stiff raft, or by the **flexible method**, treating the soil as a bed of springs of stiffness **k, the modulus of subgrade reaction**. The rigid method is simpler and conservative for stiff rafts with regular column layouts.

sections.heading: Pile foundations
sections.body:
**Classification by function**, which is what questions usually ask:

| Type | Carries load by | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **End bearing** | **Tip resistance** on a hard stratum | A firm stratum exists at reachable depth |
| **Friction (floating)** | **Shaft friction** along its length | **No firm stratum within reach** |
| **Combination** | Both | Most real piles |
| **Compaction** | Densifying loose granular soil | Ground improvement, not load transfer |
| **Tension (uplift)** | Shaft friction in tension | Resisting uplift — transmission towers, buoyant structures |
| **Batter (raker)** | Inclined, resists lateral load | Wharves, abutments |
| **Sheet** | Retains soil or water | Not a load-bearing pile |
| Anchor | Provides anchorage | — |

**Classification by material** (timber, concrete, steel, composite) and by **installation**:

| Installation | Character |
|---|---|
| **Driven (displacement)** | **Densifies** granular soil, so capacity may exceed prediction; causes **vibration and noise**; risk of damage to adjacent structures |
| **Bored (non-displacement, cast in situ)** | **No vibration**; can be taken through obstructions and inspected; but **no densification**, and quality depends on workmanship |
| Driven cast-in-situ | Casing driven, then filled |
| Jacked | No vibration, used for underpinning |

In dense urban Kathmandu, **bored piles** are usually preferred despite their cost, because driving vibration damages adjacent masonry buildings.

**Capacity:**

> **Q_u = Q_p + Q_s − W**  (end bearing + shaft friction − pile weight)
> **Q_allowable = Q_u / F**, with **F = 2.5**

In clay, **Q_p = 9 c_u A_p** and **Q_s = α c_u A_s** with the adhesion factor α ≈ 0.5–1.0. In sand, **Q_p = σ′_v N_q A_p** and **Q_s = K σ′_v tan δ A_s**.

**A caution on sand:** the end bearing does **not** grow indefinitely with depth. Beyond a **critical depth** of about 15–20 pile diameters the tip resistance becomes approximately constant, so a longer pile in uniform sand gains capacity mainly through **friction**, not end bearing.

**Pile groups.**

> **Minimum spacing 2.5 to 3 × the pile diameter** (and at least 750 mm for friction piles)

**Group efficiency** = group capacity ÷ (n × single pile capacity):

| Soil | Efficiency | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Clay** | **Less than 1** | The group acts as a **block**; the perimeter-to-area ratio falls as the group grows |
| **Dense sand** | About 1 | — |
| **Loose sand, driven piles** | **May exceed 1** | Driving **densifies** the soil between the piles |

For a group in clay the capacity must be checked **both** as the sum of individual piles **and** as an equivalent **block**, taking the **lesser**. **Converse–Labarre's formula** gives an empirical group efficiency.

**Negative skin friction — the most examined pile concept.** Where the surrounding soil settles **more than the pile**, the soil **hangs on the pile** and drags it down:

> Negative skin friction acts **DOWNWARD**. It is an **additional LOAD**, and must be **SUBTRACTED** from the pile's capacity — never added.

It arises where there is a **consolidating fill**, a **lowered water table**, or a soft clay layer consolidating under a new surcharge. Its magnitude can be very large — enough to overload a pile that appeared adequately designed. Mitigated by a **bitumen (slip) coating** on the shaft through the settling layer, by an isolation sleeve, or by designing for the extra load.

**Pile load test** (IS 2911 Part 4) is the definitive check: an **initial** test to 2.5 times the working load establishes capacity, and **routine** tests at 1.5 times on selected working piles verify construction. Safe load is taken as the lesser of that giving a **specified settlement (12 mm, or 10% of diameter for bored piles)** and **two-thirds of the load at failure**.

**Under-reamed piles** (IS 2911 Part 3) deserve mention for expansive soils: a bulb enlarged at the base provides **anchorage against uplift** when the clay swells, which a plain shaft cannot.

**Well (caisson) foundations** are used for **bridge piers in rivers**: a large hollow shaft is sunk to below the maximum scour depth by excavating within it. Components: **cutting edge, curb, steining, bottom plug, sand filling, top plug, well cap**. The **grip length** below maximum scour, typically taken as **one third of the maximum scour depth**, provides lateral stability. **Tilt and shift** during sinking are the characteristic construction problems.

formulas.label: Minimum depth of foundation (Rankine)
formulas.note: In practice not less than 0.5 m, and below seasonal moisture change, scour, frost and fill.

formulas.label: Area of an isolated footing
formulas.expression: A = total service load / net allowable bearing pressure
formulas.note: Then check one-way shear at d from the face, punching shear at d/2, bending at the face, and development length.

formulas.label: Punching (two-way) shear in a footing
formulas.expression: τ_v = V_u / (perimeter at d/2 × d) ≤ k_s · 0.25√f_ck
formulas.note: Punching shear usually governs the thickness of a footing, not bending.

formulas.label: Pile capacity
formulas.expression: Q_u = Q_p + Q_s − W ;   Q_allowable = Q_u / 2.5
formulas.note: Clay: Q_p = 9c_u A_p, Q_s = α c_u A_s. Sand: end bearing becomes constant beyond ~15–20 diameters.

formulas.label: Pile group spacing and efficiency
formulas.expression: spacing ≥ 2.5–3 d ;   efficiency = group capacity / (n × single pile capacity)
formulas.note: Less than 1 in clay (block action); may exceed 1 in loose sand because driving densifies it.

formulas.label: Negative skin friction
formulas.expression: Q_net = Q_u − Q_negative     (it acts DOWNWARD, as an added load)
formulas.note: Occurs where the soil settles more than the pile — consolidating fill, lowered water table.

formulas.label: Well foundation grip length
formulas.expression: grip length ≈ ⅓ of the maximum scour depth, below that depth
formulas.note: Provides lateral stability. Maximum scour from Lacey: R = 0.473(Q/f)^{1/3}, multiplied by 1.5–2 at a pier.
